Chapter 22: The World in My Home

Everyday Conflicts: TV Channels, Gender Rules, Honesty & Good Touch / Bad Touch

Environmental Themes, Concepts & Field Observations
  • Real-life family moral dilemmas:
  • 1. TV Channel quarrel: Tug of war between father's football, brother's cricket, sister's songs, and mother's serial.
  • 2. Gender discrimination: Pratibha must rush home by 7:00 pm, while her brothers wander freely on streets late into the night.
  • 3. Financial honesty: The kulfi vendor counts money for 5 kulfis instead of 7; Pilloo aunty honestly corrects him and pays the full price.
  • 4. Personal boundaries: Ritu avoids going to Meena's house because she feels uncomfortable around Meena's uncle (Good Touch vs Bad Touch awareness).
📖 NCERT Textbook Exercise Solutions & Step-by-Step Working (13 Solved Questions)
Q1 Why did Pilloo aunty pay the kulfi vendor for seven kulfis when he had mistakenly charged for only five? What should a child do if someone makes them feel uncomfortable by touching them? Ethics, Values & Child Safety 4 Marks
✅ Step-by-Step Model Answer & Solution:
1. Pilloo Aunty's Integrity:
The kulfi vendor was poor and made a calculation mistake in the evening rush, charging for 5 kulfis. The children thought they got two free kulfis, but Pilloo aunty immediately pointed out the error and paid for all 7 kulfis. She taught the children that taking advantage of someone's honest mistake is a form of cheating. Integrity means being fair and honest even when you could easily get away with paying less.

2. Personal Safety & Uncomfortable Touch (Child Safety Rule):
If anyone (even a familiar relative, neighbor, or stranger) touches a child in a way that feels strange, scary, or uncomfortable:
• Say a loud and firm 'NO!'
• Move away immediately from that person.
• Confide immediately in trusted adults: Mother, father, or school counselor. Never keep uncomfortable touches a secret, no matter who tells you to do so.
CBSE Step-by-Step Marking Scheme
Explains Pilloo aunty's integrity and refusal to exploit mistakes 2.0 M
Clear 3-step safety response (Say NO, Move Away, Report to Parents) 2.0 M
Q2 In Pratibha's family, her brothers could stay out late while Pratibha had to rush home by 7 PM. Why is this gender rule unjust? Gender Equity • Family Stereotypes 3 Marks
✅ Step-by-Step Model Answer & Solution:
Unjust Gender Double Standards:
Imposing early curfews exclusively on girls while allowing boys complete freedom fosters the harmful stereotype that girls are weak and boys are superior. Both boys and girls have equal rights to play, learn, and explore. True safety comes from instilling responsibility, respect, and discipline in boys, rather than curtailing girls' freedom.
CBSE Step-by-Step Marking Scheme
Critique of gender double standards 1.5 M
Equality of rights and cultivating respect in boys 1.5 M
Q3 What did Pilloo Aunty do when the beach kulfi-seller mistakenly charged her for five kulfis instead of seven? What does this teach us? Moral Values • Pilloo Aunty's Honesty 2 Marks
✅ Step-by-Step Model Answer & Solution:
Pilloo Aunty's Honesty:
The kulfi vendor was poor and made a calculation mistake, asking for money for only five kulfis. Pilloo Aunty immediately pointed out the error and paid him the full correct price for all seven kulfis.

Life Lesson:
This incident teaches children that true honesty means doing the right thing even when no one is watching, and never taking unfair advantage of someone's mistake or poverty.
CBSE Step-by-Step Marking Scheme
Factual recall of kulfi transaction 1.0 M
Ethical takeaway on integrity and fair dealing 1.0 M

Chapter 23: Pochampalli

Traditional Ikat Weaving in Mukhtarpur (Telangana), Silk Looms & Artisan Challenges

Environmental Themes, Concepts & Field Observations
  • Mukhtarpur village in Pochampalli district, Telangana: Renowned worldwide for brilliant Pochampalli Ikat handloom weaving.
  • The complete silk saree production process:
  • 1. Buying pure silk yarn bundles.
  • 2. Boiling yarn in hot water to remove dirt and impurities.
  • 3. Dyeing yarn in vibrant colors (tie-dye tieing process).
  • 4. Rolling yarn onto bobbins and fitting them onto the wooden handloom frame.
  • Threat to handloom weavers: Powerloom imitation cloth, soaring raw silk prices, greedy middlemen, and youth abandoning the craft for city jobs.
📖 NCERT Textbook Exercise Solutions & Step-by-Step Working (13 Solved Questions)
Q1 Describe the step-by-step process of weaving a Pochampalli saree. Why is this precious traditional handicraft in danger of dying out? Traditional Crafts & Economic Challenges 4 Marks
✅ Step-by-Step Model Answer & Solution:
1. The Weaving Process:
• Bundles of raw silk thread are boiled in large cauldrons to scour away grease and dirt.
• Threads are stretched onto frames and marked with intricate geometric designs. Selected sections are tied tightly with rubber strips and dipped in hot dye pots (Tie-and-Dye Ikat technique) so color penetrates only open portions.
• The colored threads are dried, rolled onto wooden bobbins, and set onto the handloom.
• Weaver artisans move the pedals and shuttles back and forth with rhythmic precision over weeks to produce a single masterpiece saree.

2. Why the Craft is in Danger:
• Skyrocketing Costs: Raw silk thread has become extremely expensive.
• Exploitation by Middlemen: Big store shopkeepers buy sarees from weavers for a meager ₹2,000 to ₹3,000 and resell them in metro cities for ₹15,000 to ₹20,000, leaving weavers impoverished.
• As a result, the younger generation is abandoning the ancestral looms to work as daily wage laborers in cities.
CBSE Step-by-Step Marking Scheme
Detailed 4-stage process (boiling, tie-dyeing, bobbin rolling, loom weaving) 2.5 M
Economic exploitation by middlemen and high silk cost 1.5 M
Q2 Describe the traditional step-by-step process of weaving a Pochampalli silk saree in Mukhtarpur village. Traditional Textiles • Pochampalli Ikat 4 Marks
✅ Step-by-Step Model Answer & Solution:
Steps in Weaving Pochampalli Saree:
1. Thread Boiling: Bundles of pure silk yarn are boiled in hot soapy water to clean impurities.
2. Tie-and-Dye (Ikat): The silk threads are marked with geometric designs, tied tightly with rubber bands, and dipped in vibrant natural dye baths so dye absorbs only in untied sections.
3. Winding on Bobbins: Dried dyed threads are rolled onto bobbins and fitted onto the wooden loom.
4. Weaving: Weavers operate the wooden foot pedals and hand shuttle back and forth for weeks to produce the lustrous geometric Pochampalli saree.
CBSE Step-by-Step Marking Scheme
Sequential four-step process (boiling, tying/dyeing, bobbins, weaving) 4.0 M
Q3 Why are many Pochampalli weaver families giving up their traditional craft to work as daily wage labourers in big cities? Artisan Livelihood • Economic Challenges 3 Marks
✅ Step-by-Step Model Answer & Solution:
Challenges Faced by Weavers:
• Skyrocketing Raw Material Costs: The price of pure mulberry silk thread and dyes has surged dramatically.
• Middlemen Exploitation: Big shopkeepers buy handloom sarees from weavers at meager prices while selling them in city showrooms at exorbitant profits.
• Powerloom Competition: Cheap polyester sarees made on machine powerlooms copy traditional Ikat designs, undercutting genuine handloom prices.
CBSE Step-by-Step Marking Scheme
Silk cost, middleman exploitation, and powerloom competition 3.0 M

Chapter 24: Home and Abroad

Abu Dhabi (UAE) vs Kerala: Deserts, Currency (Dirham), Sandstorms, Dates & Petrol

Environmental Themes, Concepts & Field Observations
  • Chittappan (uncle) and Kunjamma (aunt) return to Kerala after working five years in Abu Dhabi.
  • Geographical comparison between Abu Dhabi and Kerala:
  • 1. Climate: Abu Dhabi is a desert country—scorching heat, zero rainfall, flat sandy dunes; air-conditioners run constantly. Kerala is lush green with coconut palms, bananas, backwaters, and frequent rain.
  • 2. Vegetation: In Abu Dhabi, almost the only tree that thrives in the desert is the Date Palm (Khajoor). In Kerala, there are dense forests of jackfruit, coconut, rubber, and betel nut.
  • 3. Natural Wealth: Petrol is found in abundance underground in Abu Dhabi and is cheaper than drinking water! In Kerala, freshwater rivers flow everywhere.
  • Currency and language: Dirham (UAE currency) vs Rupee; Arabic vs Malayalam.
📖 NCERT Textbook Exercise Solutions & Step-by-Step Working (13 Solved Questions)
Q1 Why is petrol cheaper than drinking water in Abu Dhabi? What kind of tree is called the 'Date Palm' and why is it the only tree growing in deserts? Comparative Geography & Natural Resources 3 Marks
✅ Step-by-Step Model Answer & Solution:
1. Why Petrol is Cheaper than Water in Abu Dhabi:
Abu Dhabi is situated on massive subterranean reserves of crude mineral oil (petroleum), which is pumped out easily in billions of barrels. However, because it is an arid desert with zero rivers, lakes, or rainfall, fresh drinking water is extremely scarce and must be produced through expensive seawater desalination plants. Hence, underground petrol is cheaper than purified drinking water.

2. The Date Palm (Khajoor):
The Date Palm is a resilient desert tree uniquely adapted to survive in extreme sand heat with very little water. Its deep roots reach moisture, its waxy fronds prevent water loss, and it yields sweet, energy-rich dates that sustain desert populations.
CBSE Step-by-Step Marking Scheme
Abundant oil reserves vs costly seawater desalination water 1.5 M
Date palm adaptations to arid desert heat 1.5 M
Q2 Compare the geography, climate, vegetation, and natural resources of Kerala and Abu Dhabi (UAE). Comparative Geography • Kerala vs. Abu Dhabi 4 Marks
✅ Step-by-Step Model Answer & Solution:
Comparison between Kerala and Abu Dhabi:
1. Climate: Kerala has a humid, tropical climate with abundant torrential rainfall; Abu Dhabi is a scorching desert with dry heat and rarely any rain.
2. Vegetation: Kerala is carpeted with lush green coconut palms, banana trees, and paddy; Abu Dhabi has barren sand dunes where only drought-hardy date palms thrive.
3. Natural Wealth: Kerala has abundant fresh water and spices; Abu Dhabi has vast underground reserves of petroleum (crude oil), making petrol cheaper than water there.
CBSE Step-by-Step Marking Scheme
Climate, vegetation, and natural resources compared accurately 4.0 M
Q3 Why do people in Abu Dhabi wear loose white cotton robes and head scarves? Why are homes built with central air-conditioning? Desert Living • Clothing & Architecture 2 Marks
✅ Step-by-Step Model Answer & Solution:
Living in Extreme Desert Heat:
• Clothing: Men wear loose-fitting, full-length white cotton robes (Kandura) and headscarves (Ghutra) to reflect blinding sunlight, allow cooling air circulation, and shield eyes from whipping sandstorms.
• Architecture: Daytime outdoor temperatures regularly exceed 48°C. Houses are sealed with double-glazed glass to keep sand out and equipped with central air conditioning running day and night.
CBSE Step-by-Step Marking Scheme
Sun reflection, cotton air circulation, and AC architectural adaptation 2.0 M

Chapter 25: Spicy Riddles

Indian Spices (Masale): Black Pepper, Turmeric, Clove, Cumin, Cardamom & Kerala's Spice Gardens

Environmental Themes, Concepts & Field Observations
  • Kerala: The historic 'Land of Spices' (Tejpatta, Chhoti Elaichi, Badi Elaichi, Kali Mirch).
  • Spice Riddles and medicinal properties:
  • 1. Red Chilli (Lal Mirch): Sharp, spicy, makes tongue burn, watering eyes.
  • 2. Turmeric (Haldi): Bright yellow, heals cuts and wounds, mixed in hot milk for coughs.
  • 3. Black Pepper (Kali Mirch): Tiny, round, black ball, sharp and pungent, ground coarse or fine.
  • 4. Cumin (Jeera): Slender brown seeds fried in oil/ghee to scent dal; aids digestion.
  • 5. Clove (Laung): Looks like a nail with a round crown; cures severe toothache.
  • 6. Cardamom (Elaichi): Green fragrant pods that sweeten kheer and freshen breath.
📖 NCERT Textbook Exercise Solutions & Step-by-Step Working (13 Solved Questions)
Q1 Solve the riddles: (a) 'I look like a nail with a round head; put me on your aching tooth and your pain will flee.' Who am I? (b) 'I heal cuts, make food look yellow, and am mixed in milk when you cough.' Who am I? (c) Why was Kerala famous worldwide as the 'Land of Spices'? Botanical Remedies & Spices 3 Marks
✅ Step-by-Step Model Answer & Solution:
(a) Riddle 1: Clove (Laung). Its oil contains eugenol, a natural anesthetic that numbs toothache instantly.

(b) Riddle 2: Turmeric (Haldi). Its active compound curcumin has powerful anti-inflammatory and antiseptic healing properties.

(c) Why Kerala is the 'Land of Spices':
Kerala's warm tropical monsoon climate and rich Western Ghat mountain soil are ideal for growing the world's most aromatic spices—especially black pepper (known as 'Black Gold'), green cardamom, cinnamon, and cloves. Arab, Portuguese, and Dutch traders sailed across oceans for centuries to trade in Kerala spices.
CBSE Step-by-Step Marking Scheme
Solves Clove (Laung) with toothache benefit 1.0 M
Solves Turmeric (Haldi) with healing antiseptic benefit 1.0 M
Explains Kerala's historical 'Land of Spices' status 1.0 M
Q2 Match the following Indian spices with their traditional medicinal benefits:
1. Clove (Laung)
2. Turmeric (Haldi)
3. Fennel (Saunf)
4. Black Pepper (Kaali Mirch) Spices of India • Medicinal Uses 4 Marks
✅ Step-by-Step Model Answer & Solution:
Spices and Their Medicinal Benefits:
1. Clove (Laung): Looks like a tiny nail with a crown; clove oil provides instant relief from acute toothache and gum pain.
2. Turmeric (Haldi): Bright yellow antiseptic root; applied on wounds to heal cuts and mixed with warm milk to cure body aches.
3. Fennel (Saunf): Green, sweet, and cooling seeds; chewed after meals to aid digestion and freshen breath.
4. Black Pepper (Kaali Mirch): Small, round, wrinkled black bead; sharp and pungent; cures sore throats and seasonal colds.
CBSE Step-by-Step Marking Scheme
Four correct descriptions linking spice to its medicinal action 4.0 M

✅ Step-by-Step Model Answer & Solution:
Kerala - Land of Spices:
The warm, moist climate and fertile slopes of the Western Ghats in Kerala provide the perfect environment for growing world-class spices like black pepper (black gold), cardamom, cinnamon, cloves, and ginger. For thousands of years, ancient Arab, Roman, and European traders sailed across oceans to trade for Kerala's aromatic spices.

Chapter 26: Defence Officer: Wahida

Lieutenant Commander Wahida Prism, Indian Navy Doctor & Leading the Passing Out Parade

Environmental Themes, Concepts & Field Observations
  • Real-life inspiration: Lieutenant Commander Wahida Prism from Thanamandi village in Rajouri district, Jammu & Kashmir.
  • Overcoming conservative village barriers, completing MBBS from Jammu Medical College, and joining the Indian Navy.
  • Serving aboard naval warships: Naval doctors treat crew members, handle medical emergencies at sea, inspect water cleanliness, and maintain hygiene to keep the warship disease-free.
  • Historic milestone: First woman in the history of the Indian Armed Forces to lead the Annual Passing Out Parade (calling out 36 loud commands so the whole platoon hears!).
  • Why her father named her 'Prism': A glass prism reflects seven brilliant colors; her father wanted her to shine brilliantly.
📖 NCERT Textbook Exercise Solutions & Step-by-Step Working (13 Solved Questions)
Q1 Who is Wahida Prism? What are the duties of a medical officer on an Indian Navy warship, and what historic honor did she achieve during the Passing Out Parade? Inspirational Biography • Armed Forces 4 Marks
✅ Step-by-Step Model Answer & Solution:
1. Who is Wahida Prism:
Wahida Prism is an Indian Navy doctor holding the rank of Lieutenant Commander, hailing from a small village named Thanamandi in Jammu & Kashmir's Rajouri district.

2. Duties on a Naval Warship:
• Provides medical treatment and performs emergency surgeries for the entire crew sailing at sea.
• Regularly checks food and drinking water purity to prevent epidemics on the ship.
• Inspects the entire vessel daily to ensure zero rats or garbage accumulate, maintaining complete sanitation.
• Trains sailors in first aid drills and emergency casualty evacuation.

3. Historic Parade Honor:
She became the first woman officer in the history of the Indian Armed Forces to lead the prestigious Annual Passing Out Parade. Leading the parade requires immense voice projection and stamina—calling out 36 loud commands so four full platoons marching behind can hear clearly.
CBSE Step-by-Step Marking Scheme
Background of Wahida Prism from Rajouri, J&K 1.0 M
Four duties of a naval warship medical officer 1.5 M
Historic achievement of leading passing out parade with 36 commands 1.5 M
Q2 Who is Surgeon Commander Wahida Prism? Describe her journey from a small Himalayan village to an Indian Naval warship. Inspirational Careers • Wahida Prism 3 Marks
✅ Step-by-Step Model Answer & Solution:
Journey of Surgeon Commander Wahida Prism:
Wahida grew up in Thanamandi, a remote hilly village in the Rajouri district of Jammu & Kashmir. Despite conservative social pressure, her forward-thinking father supported her education. She studied diligently, completed her MBBS medical degree from Government Medical College Jammu, joined the Armed Forces, and was commissioned as a doctor in the Indian Navy, eventually serving on frontline warships and breaking glass ceilings.
CBSE Step-by-Step Marking Scheme
Humble origins in Rajouri J&K 1.5 M
MBBS medical graduation and commissioning in Indian Navy 1.5 M
Q3 Why was Wahida chosen to lead the passing-out parade at INS Hamla? Why are there 36 commands in a parade? Military Leadership • The Passing-Out Parade 3 Marks
✅ Step-by-Step Model Answer & Solution:
1. Parade Commander Selection:
Surgeon Commander Wahida was chosen to lead the prestigious annual passing-out parade because of her immaculate drill, sharp discipline, and commanding voice—becoming the first woman officer in the Indian Armed Forces to lead an entire parade.

2. The 36 Commands:
A parade commander must call out 36 loud, clear, synchronized commands without hesitation or error. The commander's voice must echo across the vast parade ground so platoons at the very rear hear each command instantly and march with split-second precision.
CBSE Step-by-Step Marking Scheme
Historical milestone as first woman parade leader 1.5 M
Importance of 36 loud commands for troop synchronization 1.5 M

Real-World Environment Context: Wahida's father gave her the unique middle name 'Prism' when she was a little girl.

Chapter 27: Chuskit Goes to School

Inclusivity in Skitpo Pul (Ladakh), Overcoming Wheelchair Barriers & Community Bridge Building

Environmental Themes, Concepts & Field Observations
  • Chuskit: A 9-year-old girl born with impaired legs who lives in Skitpo Pul village in Ladakh.
  • Her dream: Yearning to go to school like her younger brother, carry a school bag, and make friends.
  • The physical barrier: An uneven rocky mountain path and a roaring glacial stream with no bridge preventing her wheelchair from passing.
  • Empathy in action: Her schoolmate Abdul notices her sorrow, meets the Headmaster and teachers, and convinces them to make the path accessible.
  • Community bridge-building: Schoolchildren and villagers unite with shovels, level the rocky slope, build a wooden plank bridge over the stream, and roll Chuskit's wheelchair into school amidst joyful cheers!
📖 NCERT Textbook Exercise Solutions & Step-by-Step Working (13 Solved Questions)
Q1 Why had 9-year-old Chuskit never attended school before? How did Abdul, the teachers, and school children work together to make her dream come true? Inclusive Education & Community Action 4 Marks
✅ Step-by-Step Model Answer & Solution:
1. Why Chuskit couldn't attend school:
Chuskit could not use her legs since birth and moved around using a wheelchair. Although her school was not far away across the hill, the pathway was steep, bumpy, and strewn with sharp rocks. Worst of all, there was a fast-flowing glacial stream that had no bridge. A wheelchair could not roll across the rocks or cross the stream, so her grandfather sadly believed school was impossible for her.

2. How Abdul and the School Solved the Problem:
Abdul, a compassionate schoolboy, spoke passionately with the Headmaster and teachers, pointing out that Chuskit had every right to study. The Headmaster called a meeting: one group of students and villagers took shovels and leveled the uneven rocky road smooth; another group cut flat wooden planks and constructed a sturdy bridge across the roaring stream. With the path made barrier-free, Chuskit wheeled into the schoolyard to the cheering applause of all teachers and children.
CBSE Step-by-Step Marking Scheme
Physical obstacles explained (rocky slope and roaring stream without bridge) 2.0 M
Abdul's initiative and community collective labor to build bridge and level road 2.0 M
Q2 How did Abdul mobilize the school headmaster and children to make Chuskit's dream of going to school come true? Inclusive Education • The Bridge for Chuskit 3 Marks
✅ Step-by-Step Model Answer & Solution:
Community Action for Chuskit:
Abdul spoke to the school headmaster and teachers, explaining that Chuskit was intelligent and eager to study. The headmaster organized a school work-project: one group of children cleared and leveled the jagged stones on the riverside path, while another group placed flat wooden planks across the fast-flowing stream to build a level bridge. Working together, they created a smooth path so Chuskit's wheelchair could roll straight into the school courtyard.
CBSE Step-by-Step Marking Scheme
Abdul's initiative with the headmaster 1.5 M
Children clearing rocks and laying wooden bridge planks 1.5 M
Q3 What does 'Inclusive Education' mean? Why must every school be barrier-free for children with special needs? Constitutional Values • Inclusive Schools 3 Marks
✅ Step-by-Step Model Answer & Solution:
Inclusive Education:
Inclusive education means that children with special physical or cognitive needs study alongside their peers in regular mainstream classrooms, rather than being isolated in separate institutions.

Need for Barrier-Free Infrastructure:
Under the Right to Education (RTE) Act and the Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, every child has a legal and moral right to education. Installing ramps, wide doorways, Braille signage, and accessible toilets ensures that physical disability never becomes a barrier to learning and thriving.
CBSE Step-by-Step Marking Scheme
Definition of inclusive mainstream education 1.5 M
Barrier-free ramps and RTE constitutional rights 1.5 M

🌟 NEP 2020 Competency-Based Case Study (CBQ)

Building an Accessible Barrier-Free School

Real-World Environment Context: Even today, many schools have flights of stairs at entrances and narrow classroom doors that block wheelchairs.

Analytical Task: What three modifications must every school make to become truly inclusive for children with mobility disabilities?

1. Gentle Ramps with Handrails: Alongside all staircases and entrances.
2. Wide Level Doors: At least 90 cm wide with zero raised floor thresholds for wheelchairs to roll easily.
3. Accessible Restrooms: Toilets with grab bars, wide cubicle doors, and low sinks.
CBSE Assessment Rubric: 1.0 Mark for ramps with handrails; 1.0 Mark for wide doors; 1.0 Mark for accessible restrooms.
